newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria's economic outlook mixed after budget.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria's economic outlook mixed after budget.

text.p: Nigeria's economy should grow moderately in 1997 despite a disappointing government budget which includes targets which seem unachievable, senior business executives said at a post-budget seminar on Wednesday.
Disappointment stems mainly from a delay in privatising loss-making but potentially profitable state enterprises and from the failure to merge the dual naira exchange rates.

Business and international institutions have criticised Nigeria's system which allows the government access to foreign exchange at a preferential rate of 22 naira to the U.S. dollar, compared with 80 naira per dollar at central bank auctions.
The military government had earlier raised investors' hopes of action in 1997 both on privatisation and on unifying exchange rates.

"The prospects for growth in 1997 hinge on efficient public sector investment spending," Wale Edun, managing director of investment house Denham Management Ltd told the seminar organised by Arthur Anderson business consultants in Lagos.
"If agriculture grows, and oil and gas go the way they have been doing, then we could meet the target growth of 5.5 percent," he added.

The budget, presented last week, shifts government spending dramatically to rural areas and towards restoring a deteriorating public infrastructure, which the government hopes will have a positive impact on living conditions in the villages.

As a result, the government expects gross domestic product to grow by 5.5 percent compared to 3.25 percent last year, and that the economic stability of the last two years will continue with the naira currency appreciating in order to achieve a merger of the official and free market rates.

"Given the expansionary nature of the 1997 monetary policies, it is difficult to see how a sustainable appreciation in the value of the naira will be achieved," said Tayo Aderinokun, deputy managing director of Guaranty Trust Bank Plc.
The economy hit turbulence after June 1993 when a previous army government annulled a presidential poll aimed at restoring democracy.
Wealthy businessman Moshood Abiola, the man widely believed to have won the annulled vote, is in jail awaiting trial for proclaiming himself president in defiance of the army rulers.

The seminar was silent on the political crisis precipitated in Nigeria since the election annulment. In the last two months three bomb blasts linked to the crisis have rocked Lagos, killing three soldiers and injuring dozens.

Participants at the Lagos seminar expressed worry that the government had postponed privatisation, saying it was unlikely the policy would be carried out in 1998 when the government would be preoccupied with its pledge to arrange presidential elections.
But they said Nigeria must carefully prepare its vast oil industry, especially the problem refineries, for privatisation.

"As far as the refineries are concerned privatisation is the only way out and I don't think it is on the backburner," said Jide Soyeye, a former general manager of the Warri refinery and now an energy consultant.

"The government is wise to say it wants to study it more carefully and I think the first thing to do is to free the pricing of oil products to market forces to make the refineries profitable, otherwise no investor will come," he added.
Bankers at the seminar hailed the requirement on banks to raise their share capital to a minimum of 500 million naira ($6.25 million) by the end of 1998 from 50 million naira now.
"This will fundamentally reshape the banking industry and position it to effectively compete for the future," said Aderinokun.
